opening.headline: To build agents that remember user preferences even after a session ends, learn the structure and write policies for external memory that stores information outside the context.
body: In the first session, the user said, "Please keep the response short and summarize it in a table." However, when the next session begins, the agent doesn't know about this preference. If we include all past conversations in the context, the context becomes too large and costs increase.

This course covers external memory by storing only what is necessary outside the context and retrieving it when needed. It compares memory tools that read and write files with management-based Memory Banks that extract and integrate information during conversations, and distinguishes between session state and long-term memory. It also highlights risks associated with personal data remaining in memory through illustrative examples.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe memory tools and the structure of Memory Bank
Distinguish between session state and long-term memory

screens.title: The session should remember the user's preferences even after it ends.
screens.lead: Please read the scene of the conversation spanning two sessions. The diagram illustrates how information mentioned in Session 1 disappears in Session 2.

visual.alt: A diagram showing two conversation windows starting in an unknown state to the agent, where the user request from session 1 is not forwarded to session 2.
labels: Keep the answer brief and organize it in a table.
Tell me this month's sales figure.
Once the session ends, the context is lost.

paragraphs: In session 1, the user asked the agent to briefly summarize the response in a table format. The agent complied with this request. However, when the session ends, the conversation context is lost. When session 2 begins, the agent does not know the user's preference and responds in a lengthy paragraph format.

We could include all past conversations in the context to resolve this. Then the context would become full, turn costs would increase, and questions would be posed within lengthy conversations requiring substantial information. Context has finite resources.

External memory is a method where only necessary information is stored outside the context and retrieved when needed. This lesson covers two implementations: one is a memory tool that allows the model to read from and write to files, and the other is a Memory Bank that extracts and manages meaningful information during a conversation.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: To remember is not only about storing information, but also about deciding what not to store.

screens.outro: Let us consider whether an agent requires long-term memory.

screens.title: Think of an agent that requires long-term memory
screens.lead: After first thinking through the question mentally and making a choice, the instructor's thought process is revealed. Answers are not entered or submitted.

items.prompt: What kind of agent requires long-term memory?
items.answer: Customer support agents benefit from remembering a customer's past inquiries and preferences, coding agents from recalling project rules and past decisions, and personal assistants from remembering scheduling habits and preferred communication styles. The commonality across all three is that they interact with the same person or project over multiple sessions.

items.prompt: What should that agent remember and what should it forget?
items.answer: What to remember are preferred facts, decisions, and information repeatedly used. What to forget are one-time trivialities, outdated and incorrect information, and sensitive data that has no need for storage. This distinction serves as the starting point for writing policies.

items.prompt: What happens if memory is incorrectly stored?
items.answer: If incorrect content is stored, all subsequent sessions inherit that error. Personal information that is stored increases the risk of unintended exposure. While storage is easy, the difficulty in recovering from it constitutes a burden in memory design.

screens.outro: First, we will distinguish between session state and long-term memory.

screens.title: Distinction between session state and long-term memory
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare how the storage's lifespan, storage location, and search method differ.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the difference in lifetime between session state within a conversation and long-term memory spanning multiple sessions.

tabs.label: session state
tabs.body: In ADK, a Session contains the record of events and temporary state data for a single conversation. It represents short-term memory within a specific conversation. Once the conversation ends, this record is not automatically reused in another session.

tabs.label: MemoryService
tabs.body: Long-term memory is a searchable repository that stores knowledge from previous conversations or other sources. ADK's MemoryService adds completed sessions to the long-term storage via add_session_to_memory, and the agent typically retrieves relevant fragments through search_memory using tools. It only loads the necessary parts, thus maintaining context awareness.

tabs.label: Implementation selection
tabs.body: ADK's Python implementation consists of three versions. InMemoryMemoryService loses data upon restart and only performs basic keyword matching, making it suitable for prototypes and local testing. VertexAiMemoryBankService extracts meaningful information from conversations, integrates it with existing memory, and supports semantic search. VertexAiRagMemoryService performs search by vector similarity across the entire conversation.

tabs.label: Memory Bank
tabs.body: Memory Bank is a managed service that creates long-term memory based on the conversation between the user and the agent, maintaining it across multiple sessions. It preserves isolated memory collections per scope, ensuring that users' memories do not mix. Each memory is an independent and self-contained piece of information.

screens.outro: Now let's read about how file-based memory tools are actually invoked.

screens.title: Memory tools: reading requests and results
screens.lead: This is the configuration and invocation flow of Claude memory tools. Select the descriptions beside each line to verify who is performing what.

visual.alt: A flow where the model requests a memory tool and the application executes it from storage, returning the result.
labels: Map the path to the actual storage repository

notes.note: The setting to enable the memory tool is this one line. The name must be "memory", and the input schema is not defined separately. When enabled, the model automatically checks the memory directory before starting a task.

This is a tool call generated by the model. Since the command is "view" and the path is "/memories", it means the model intends to first inspect the directory before proceeding with the operation. The model only makes the request; the actual execution is handled by the application.

This is the tool_result returned by the application. The content includes a file list and sizes under the /memories path. The side that creates this list is not the model but the handler, and the storage location is determined by the developer.

This is a subsequent call that selects and reads only the files needed by the model. It uses a JIT (Just-In-Time) approach where files are loaded only when required, rather than reading all of them at once. The commands include view, create, str_replace, insert, delete, and rename.

Be cautious when the path value points outside of /memories. /memories is a prefix path that maps to user-specific directories or DB keys. If a handler does not reject paths pointing outside of /memories, there is a risk of path traversal that could allow access to files belonging to other users.

screens.outro: Having examined the tool-based approach, let us now look at the writing policy of the management-based approach.

screens.title: Memory Bank and Write Policy
screens.lead: The following is an example of a single memory entry managed by a Memory Bank for a single user. When an emphasized section is selected, a description appears explaining which of extraction, integration, or scope it relates to.

data.text: scope: agent_name="Order Notification Agent", user="User A" / fact: User A prefers to receive responses briefly and in tabular format.. / generation method: after conversation ends, Generated asynchronously in the background / extraction topic: Preferred and decision-limited / integration: if newly acquired preference differs from existing memory, Update existing memory

marks.span: scope: agent_name="Order Notification Agent", user="User A"
marks.note: This is the scope. A Memory Bank maintains an isolated collection of memories per scope, so that memories from other users do not mix. Memory searches must also occur solely within the scope.

marks.span: User A prefers to receive responses briefly and in tabular format.
marks.note: It is a fact. An independent piece of information containing only the most meaningful information, not the entire original conversation. The output of the extraction process.
This approach handles memory generation behind the scenes such that it does not delay the agent's response. Instead, the just-said statement may not be immediately reflected in memory.
What it means can be customized using the topic and few-shot examples. Narrowing down the storage target is the core of the writing policy and reduces unnecessary information and risks.
It is integration. Newly extracted information is combined with existing memories, enabling memories to evolve. Simply stacking all statements results in contradictory memories.

screens.outro: Let's illustrate the risks that arise when a write policy is inadequate, using a concrete example.

screens.title: Explanation: Risk of personal data remaining in memory
screens.lead: The instructor walks through the process step by step of identifying and correcting risks in the memory of customer support agents. Select the right arrow to follow along.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: Contact information and addresses have been accumulated as facts in the customer support agent's memory. One day, a memory access request from the model displayed the path "path": "/memories/../other_user/profile.xml". Let's examine each of these requests and stored contents in terms of the risks they represent.

steps.title: Step 1: Read the path line
steps.body: The path attempts to go beyond the /memories prefix. Since memory tools run on the client side, the handler must restrict all operations to within /memories and reject paths that point outside of it. Without such rejection logic, another user's files would be read directly.

steps.title: Step 2: Read stored fact
steps.body: If personal information such as contact details and addresses is stored, there is a risk that this data may be retrieved and exposed again in other conversations. While storage occurs only once, searches can happen multiple times, continuously increasing the exposure risk. The safest approach is to avoid storing unnecessary information from the outset.

steps.title: Step 3: Scope Verification
steps.body: If scopes are not isolated by user, memories from different users get mixed. Memory Bank maintains a segregated collection of memories per scope, and ADK's memory search is restricted to the user-level identification scope. In file-based approach, /memories is mapped to user-specific directories to achieve the same effect.

steps.title: Improvement 1: Fix the handler
steps.body: The handler rejects paths pointing outside /memories and maps prefix paths to user-specific stores. Even if the request originates from a model, the path is always validated before execution. The model's output is not trustworthy input.

steps.title: Improvement 2: Define Write Policy
steps.body: Limit the extraction topics to preferences and decisions, and exclude sensitive information from storage. Predefine retention periods and deletion pathways. It must be specified in advance how data will be erased when a user requests memory deletion. All of this constitutes a write policy that simultaneously defines memory quality and security.

steps.title: Improvement 3: Deletion and Retention Period
steps.body: The retention period of stored memories and the method for deletion when requested by the user are defined. In file-based systems, files can be organized using delete and rename commands, while managed services handle memories at the memory unit level. Additionally, during the integration phase, existing memories are updated to ensure outdated or corrupted information is not retained.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: The risk in memory lies not in the storage method, but in the absence of write policies and access controls. First, you must determine what is stored, who has access, and when data is deleted—whether using a file-based or managed approach. Memory without policies becomes debt rather than memory. Policies must be defined before they are implemented.

screens.outro: We will conclude by summarizing the core point in one sentence.

screens.title: Core takeaway: Memory quality is determined by its write policy
screens.lead: Establishing criteria for external memory design.

paragraphs: Session state acts as short-term memory for a conversation, while long-term memory serves as a retrievable repository that persists beyond the session. Long-term memory includes memory tools such as file read-and-write capabilities, as well as managed services like a Memory Bank that extracts and integrates meaningful information from conversations. Regardless of the approach, agents retrieve information only when needed, without keeping all content in context.

The quality of memory is determined not by storage technology but by write policies. The core of these policies lies in what is stored (limited to preferences and decisions), who's scope it belongs to (user-level isolation), and when it is refreshed and deleted (integration and removal). In tool-based approaches, the application itself manages storage locations and execution, so policies also include rejecting paths that point outside of /memories.

List three things your agent should remember and three things it should not remember. These two lists form the initial draft of a writing policy. Having such lists enables judgment about what to store and what to block, regardless of which storage system is used.

Finally, we must consider the locus of responsibility. Memory tools directly manage storage, so path validation and access control become the developer's responsibility; in contrast, managed services shift the responsibility to the developer for determining what it means for the service to handle storage and retrieval. Regardless of the approach chosen, the responsibility for defining policies does not vanish. As long as there is a policy document, the implementation can be changed while maintaining the same standards.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Memory that stores all conversations is not good memory. Memory that retains only meaningful information is good memory.

glossary.def: A client-side tool that creates, reads, modifies, deletes files in the /memories directory and preserves information across sessions.
A managed long-term memory repository that extracts and integrates meaningful information from conversations and preserves it beyond the session.
It involves finding relevant memories within the identification scope and bringing them into the context.
Rules for determining when, what, and how to store and erase memories.

misconceptions.fact: You should extract only meaningful information to achieve high quality and reduce risks. Accumulating all conversations also accumulates contradictions and risks of personal data exposure.

misconceptions.myth: Session state and long-term memory are the same thing.
misconceptions.fact: Session state is short-term memory for a single conversation, while long-term memory is a repository accessible beyond the session for retrieval.

misconceptions.myth: Memory tools automatically handle the storage.
misconceptions.fact: Memory tools only generate requests; storage location and actual execution are handled by the application.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Session state is short-term memory, while long-term memory persists beyond the session.
Memory tools operate in a file read-and-write manner, while Memory Bank manages extraction and integration.
Limits the target and scope, and rejects paths outside of memories, reducing risk.
